entries.title: Cubs’ offense backs Jameson Taillon's solid start
entries.summary: <p>SAN DIEGO — Jameson Taillon spent part of Wednesday morning giving an impromptu concert with guitars stashed in the visitors’ clubhouse at Petco Park.</p><p>Given how well he pitched, setting down the first 14 batters in order, surviving two solo homers, and then allowing just one more hit in seven innings of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>’ 5-4 victory over the Padres, should we expect an encore from the music man?</p><p>“No, there’s no guitars anywhere else other than here,’’ Taillon said. “So we’re safe.</p><p>“They’re Taylor guitars, really, really nice, actually. I mean, I haven’t played in like 10 years, but I used to play a bunch, and I know about 4½ songs.’’</p><p>His signature tune?</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-floatRight><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/C-Naa1HXeDQ?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Matchbox Twenty - 3AM (Official Video) [HD Remaster]"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>“3AM by Matchbox Twenty,’’ he said.</p><p>Fourteen up, fourteen down is generally too early to be thinking about 27 up, 27 down. Taillon was aware that no one had reached base. “More than anything, I was aware I had good stuff today and good command, good pitch mix,’’ he said.</p><p>The Cubs and Padres played each other in a NL wild-card series last October, the Cubs taking two out of three, with all three games played in Wrigley because the Cubs finished with a better regular season record. Taking two out of three in Petco, and finishing 3-3 in this six-game trip against the best in the West, the Dodgers and Padres, even if it’s April, made for a satisfying flight home.</p><p>Ben Brown assured the Cubs of a happy landing by inheriting a bases-loaded, no-out situation in the eighth and allowing just one run, on a sacrifice fly by Fernando Tatis Jr. Brown subsequently induced a double-play ground ball from Manny Machado, stand-in second baseman Matt Shaw turning two to end the inning.</p><p>Home runs by Shaw, who fell a triple short of the cycle (bunt single in the fourth, double in the sixth), and Pete Crow-Armstrong, his second in two games, proved decisive.</p><p>“I mean, he impacts the game no matter what,’’ Taillon said. “Even if the bat’s not there, he’s making a difference running the bases and playing defense with the energy he brings, but when the bat’s going, it’s a game changer. He can electrify an offense.’’</p><p>Former Cubs pitcher and broadcaster Rick Sutcliffe said he spoke with injured pitcher Justin Steele [strained flexor] by phone Wednesday. “We talked a little, cried a little,’’ Sutcliffe said. “He had an injection. They’ll have to wait three or four weeks for the inflammation to go down. Things were going so well. I just told him this team is built for October. Get back here by September 1 and get after it.’’</p><p>Padres pitchers threw at least five pitches that were dangerously wild the last two games. Shaw was knocked down Tuesday and had a pitch go behind him Wednesday, Seiya Suzuki was knocked down Tuesday, and Nico Hoerner was hit by a pitch in the brim of his helmet. “I’ve never seen so many balls high and tight in a series, right?” Shaw said. “I mean, there’s certain times maybe guys are doing it on purpose, but it was never like that here today. entries.title: Cubs manager Craig Counsell celebrates 900th MLB victory
entries.summary: <p>SAN DIEGO — The bitter taste of victory?</p><p>How else to describe the shot of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/7/8/23787109/malort-jeppsons-unlikely-rise-liquor-alcohol-wormwood" >Jeppson’s Malört </a>that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> players and staff insisted Craig Counsell share with them on the occasion of his 900th win as a major-league manager Tuesday night.</p><p>A helpful member of the Cubs’ traveling party made sure to have the libation on hand, which has become<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/entertainment-and-culture/2021/8/25/22641237/what-does-malort-taste-like-chicago-liquor" > a cult favorite</a> in Chicago establishments that serve adult beverages, even though it has been described as a “famously disgusting liqueur from Chicago.”</p><p>Counsell, a Wisconsinite savvy enough to avoid offending the local citizenry, did not share his opinion. Instead, he offered a couple of thoughts on what it meant to reach the round number that leaves him No. 78 on the all-time managers list — nine wins behind Jimy Williams after win No. 901 on Wednesday — and fifth on the list of active managers (The Reds’ Terry Francona ranks No. 1 with 2,051 entering Wednesday).</p><p>“Mostly, I think you think about players No. 1, and then probably that you’ve just been in the game for a long time,’’ he told the reporters gathered in his office. “You’ve been doing it for a while, and fortunate to be doing it for a long time.</p><p>“. . . You think of players going through this journey of their career, like [reliever] Ryan Rolison getting their shot in the last couple of days and doing a heck of a job. Those are the rewarding moments. . . . Those are the things that you’re happy about and proud of as you go through this.’’</p><p>Earlier Tuesday, Counsell sat on a dugout bench and talked about those who helped him along the way — Pat Murphy, his coach at Notre Dame and then his bench coach in Milwaukee; Jim Leyland, his first manager in the big leagues; and Bob Melvin, who managed him in Arizona.</p><p>“[Melvin] let me, you know, behind the curtain,’’ Counsell told the Sun-Times, “a little bit into what his job was like. He gave me a lot of freedom as a player. And he always talked<br>to me about why you did it and why you don’t, what he was thinking. He definitely exposed me to a little more.’’</p><p>Counsell is 55 now, an age where you are more likely to be mentor than mentee.</p><p>“I think when you get older, you look forward to sharing more, but you’re still learning,’’ said Counsell, who received congratulations from several members of the managing fraternity, including Alex Cora.</p><p>“So you’re still learning a lot, so I don’t think that changes. There’s still things you can learn and be better at. That never stops.’’</p><p>There are no seminars or weekend retreats for big-league managers. Generally, the only time they’re all together in one place is during the winter meetings, but much of that time is spent plotting trades and free-agent signings.</p><p>Counsell said he talks fairly regularly with other managers by phone.</p><p>“You’re definitely in relationships with some of these guys,’’ he said. “. . . If you’ve this done for a while, maybe you’re not close friends with some of these guys, but you’re checking on them, they’re checking on you, and you run questions by them.’’</p><p>Then there are interactions with coaches from other sports. Counsell tends to favor basketball coaches. While in San Diego, he visited with the basketball coaches at the University of San Diego.</p><p>“I think the coaches from other sports, they share a lot of the same concepts,’’ he said. “You’re managing people, you’re managing up [to management] and down [to players], so to speak. That’s probably the biggest commonality.’’</p><p>He finds material on social media posted by coaches useful. “Like Kara Lawson, the women’s basketball coach at Duke,’’ he said. “She’s awesome with stuff.’’</p><p>Counsell is not into reading leadership or self-help books. “When I read,’’ he said, “it’s usually fiction. I do it more to get away from the game.’’</p><p>As for the current emphasis on analytics? “I don’t like that word,’’ he said. “I prefer calling it information. How are people using information.’’</p><p>Absorbing the information, then conveying it. He finds that the degree in accounting he earned at Notre Dame has proven useful. How good an accountant would he have been?</p><p>“It wasn’t a life goal to be an accountant,’’ he said.</p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-hide-descriptions="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a class="AnchorLink" id="list-c90005" name="list-c90005"></a><div class="PageList-header" > <div class="PageList-header-title-wrap" > <div class="PageList-header-title"> <a class="" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="{borderColor=#dfdfdf, pageNumber=1, count=13868, titleUrl=https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs, inverseColors=false, pagination=[{body=[Next Page], href=?p=2, _template=/link/Link.hbs, contentId=null, pianoSectionSlug=null, target=null}], pullQuoteIcon=[{image=null, narrowImage=null, _template=/image/Image.hbs, alt=null}], footerBgColor=#000000, title=Latest on the Cubs, bodyFont=font-3, showListNumbers=false, imagePositionHorizontal=null, rteBodyFont=font-3, headerBottomBorderColor=#111010, subTitle=null, stickyHeader=true, listTitleColor=#000000, tableCellBorderColor=#ccd1d5, relatedListFont=font-1, hideAuthors=true, tertiaryTextColor=#6c6c6c, buttonHoverTextColor=#ffffff, tableFont=font-1, carouselAutoPlay=false, promoTitleFont=font-2, ctaButtonText=[], primaryTextColor=#2a2a2a, buttonTextColor=#ffffff, linkTextColor=#1a1a1a, hideTitles=false, footerLinkColor=#ffffff, items=[{type=Image, description=[{items=[Counsell credits former players and coaches on his career mark. entries.title: After two years in Chicago, the Angel Reese era now feels like a dream
entries.summary: <p>Was it all a dream?</p><p>When Angel Reese was drafted No. 7 in 2024, it felt like a new day in Chicago. The world's attention was turning toward women's basketball, and now, blessed with one of the sport's biggest names, Chicago would be at the epicenter.</p><p>Reese had her naysayers coming out of LSU, but she proved many of them wrong.</p><p>Her game, it turned out, translated to the pros. In her rookie season, she surpassed Sylvia Fowles to claim the single-season rebounding record and set a WNBA mark for the most consecutive double-doubles with 15.</p><p>There was still a lot of room for growth, sure, but it looked like she had the potential to be the face of the franchise. </p><p>It wasn't just that she was a generational rebounder with All-Defense potential and MVP aspirations.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/04/29/angel-reese-is-living-the-dream-in-atlanta-and-this-match-might-be-built-to-last" >Greenberg: Angel Reese is living the dream in Atlanta — and this match might be built to last</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>It was also that she was the kind of larger-than-life figure the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> had not had since Candace Parker. She was the kind of star who ensured celebrities sat courtside at Wintrust — the kind who could hit the Met Gala on a Monday and help down the Liberty on a Tuesday.</p><p>That meant something. Players who change franchises don't just produce; they project their personality. Reese had the necessary flair: she was unapologetic, multi-dimensional, a fierce competitor.</p><p>There was a certain grace in the fact that she wanted to be in Chicago. The Sky had struggled since the 2021 championship core split and head coach James Wade departed abruptly during the 2023 season. But Reese embraced the opportunity. She wanted to play for Teresa Weatherspoon, a WNBA legend and first-time head coach, and the city rallied around them in 2024.</p><p>But the fame and the spotlight Reese carries also embedded a tension into the partnership with the Sky. While Reese pulled Chicago into the WNBA's modern era, the Sky remained relative stragglers on the organizational side.</p><p>As franchises in New York, Phoenix, Minnesota and Las Vegas began operating more like NBA teams, the Sky still lacked a dedicated practice facility, a robust performance staff, and an in-house analytics team. </p><p>Still, Reese defended them. She told reporters at media day in 2025 that while people want to start with the "glitz and the glamour," you sometimes have to "start in the gutter."</p><p>Maybe Reese and the Sky could evolve together. Growing pains and all.</p><p>Reese's second season had plenty of them. She endured an epic slump to start the year, struggling to finish around the rim and looking hesitant with her outside shot. But she played herself out of it, adapting to coach Tyler Marsh's system and showing she could be a playmaker and a ballhandler, too.</p><p>Meanwhile, the Sky were headed toward one of their worst seasons in franchise history, weighed down by injuries and a talent deficit. Organizationally, they were trying to elevate the player experience, but the reality of practicing in a public recreation center overshadowed other changes.</p><p>By the end of the season, Reese's public comments suggested she was far less satisfied with the view from the gutter.</p><p>On the Sky's facilities: "Y'all saw the rec where we practice at … I don't think anyone wants to practice there."</p><p>On their roster: "I'm not settling for the same s— we did this year," Reese told the Tribune. "We have to get good players. We have to get great players. That's a non-negotiable for me."</p><p>The Sky ultimately suspended Reese for a half-game for comments she made in the Tribune interview, and she sat out the remainder of the season with a back injury.</p><p>The relationship hit a crossroads. Could Reese still be a foundational piece? A pillar? Somewhere in between? Then, poof, she was gone.</p><p>To hear both sides tell it now, it is almost as if the era never happened. Both insist it was a mutual parting: no trade request, no love lost. Just a general manager <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/04/22/will-this-time-be-different-sky-push-for-a-fresh-start" >making an opportunistic move</a>, just a player doing what was best for her career.</p><p>"There's a lot of gray area in basketball and trading and there's no black and white answer of this is right and this is wrong," Sky guard Hailey Van Lith said before Wednesday's preseason game against the Dream. "People just go with their gut and I think that's kind of what played out. It's a gray area, and you have respect for everyone involved and you keep pushing."</p><p>The Dream won the gray area Wednesday night, 87-78, with Reese looking like what her new teammates have been calling "the missing piece." </p><p>What's possible for this Dream team in the regular season?</p><p>"I think what's possible is ultimately win a championship," coach Karl Smesko said before the game.</p><p>What's possible for the Sky?</p><p>It's still tough to get a good read. On paper they look like a playoff-caliber team, but three of their major offseason signings—Azurá Stevens, Courtney Vandersloot and DiJonai Carrington—are all out with injuries and lack specific return timelines.</p><p>The Sky do have candidates for the face-of-the-franchise question in Rickea Jackson and Kamilla Cardoso. They’ve also taken steps to professionalize, now practicing at UIC’s Flames Athletic Center and adding a performance staff.</p><p>But there's plenty of gray area left to work entries.title: Angel Reese is living the dream in Atlanta — and this match might be built to last
entries.summary: <p>No defensiveness. No dismissiveness. No unpleasantness.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/04/28/sky-angel-reese-strike-friendly-tone-ahead-of-preseason-matchup" target="_blank" >Angel Reese</a> answered the questions that had to be asked Wednesday, and the new face of the Atlanta Dream handled them like a pro’s pro.</p><p>She can’t be thrilled with how her two years with the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> ended — after all that losing and with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2025/09/05/sky-suspend-angel-reese-for-first-half-of-aces-game" target="_blank" >acrimony between superstar and team</a> — can she?</p><p>“I’m still happy,” she said. “I’m grateful for my time here in Chicago — I experienced a lot of great things — but I’m just happy to start this new journey.”</p><p>Why didn’t things work out better between the “Bayou Barbie” and the team that drafted her in 2024, which she publicly took to task for some of its glaring weaknesses late last season?</p><p>“I think it was just best for me to move on, and I think it was helpful for both of us,” she said. “I’m grateful for Chicago for putting me in a [trade with Atlanta] where I can come somewhere that I really wanted and people really wanted me. I’m just grateful to turn the page. No love lost.”</p><p>Did returning to Wintrust Arena for an exhibition game in her old backyard remind her just how permanently she hopes to make the Sky rue the day they called it a wrap and dealt her?</p><p>“It’s just like any game,” she said. “I’m just looking forward to another opportunity to play basketball.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/04/06/sky-trade-angel-reese-to-atlanta-dream-for-2027-2028-draft-picks" >Sky trade Angel Reese to Dream for first-round draft picks in 2027, 2028</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/04/09/angel-reese-after-trade-i-just-feel-that-urge-right-now-that-im-going-to-win-again" target="_blank" >Angel Reese after trade: ‘I just feel that urge right now that I’m going to win again’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Oh, and how happy is “happy” as she moves forward with one of the best — and most functional — organizations in the WNBA?</p><p>“I’ve shown all 32 teeth every day,” she said.</p><p>That’s 32 more than I saw the first time I attempted to interview her, early in her rookie season. That day, after a practice in Deerfield, she turned her back to me, said she didn’t trust me and accused me of aiming to twist her words, all of which was a bit strange given we’d never met. Then again, she didn’t owe me anything more than that considering the way basketball “fans” were abusing her online and some in the broadly defined “media” wanted to pigeonhole her as an enemy of Caitlin Clark.</p><p>Reese got through her time in Chicago, but it never seemed as enjoyable for her or rich with possibilities as it does in Atlanta, where the Dream are coming off a 30-14 season — 20 games better than the bumbling Sky were in the standings — and are right behind the Liberty, Aces and Fever among this year’s championship favorites.</p><p>An 87-78 exhibition win against the Sky didn’t mean much in the scheme of things, but Reese’s inability to wipe a smile off her face during warmups just might. Surrounded by serious talent — Rhyne Howard, Allisha Gray, Brionna Jones, Jordin Canada, Naz Hillmon — she has a chance not only to win but also to be the reason the Dream ascend to a new level.</p><p>Reese didn’t exactly look different in her first action with the Dream, missing some close-in shots and pounding the glass — her signatures with the Sky — but her level of intensity stood out, and that’s a good sign. Her enthusiasm with her new teammates did, too, including on the bench in the second half when, her night’s work done, she took on the role of lead cheerleader. It isn’t difficult at all to imagine these attributes being factors that send the Dream over the top.</p><p>“My first impression is she’s an All-Star-level player already, and I think she has some room to grow because she’s only been in the league a couple years,” Dream coach Karl Smesko said. “And I don’t think she’s satisfied with where she’s at. She wants to be one of the very best players in the league, and I think she has that potential.”</p><p>Reese will turn 24 four days before the Dream’s regular-season opener. It could be a tailor-made scenario for her on a team with such healthy vibes — completely unlike recent Sky squads — that Howard, Gray, Jones, Canada and Hillmon all re-signed as free agents despite a Wild West offseason of opportunity throughout the league.</p><p>Then again, Reese does have to work her way into an established culture, which can be harder than it sounds. It’s too soon for anyone to say she has already managed that.</p><p>But as a giddy Reese put it in a recent scrum with reporters in Atlanta, “It feels great. I mean, I can’t believe this is my life.”</p><p>If the Sky ever made her feel like that, we must have missed it.</p><p></p><p></p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module entries.title: Pete Kastanes, who spread nostalgia with Vanished Chicagoland social media posts, dies at 62
entries.summary: <p></p><p></p><p></p><p>For Pete Kastanes, nostalgia was like salt — properly sprinkled, it made everything better.</p><p>He liked to leaf through high school yearbooks and collect old comics. </p><p>His matchbook collection evoked images of neon bar signs.</p><p>His DVD collection leaned into old Disney capers featuring a young Hayley Mills. "That Darn Cat!" was one of his favorites.</p><p>As a kid, he wanted to go see things in Chicago that he'd heard about, like pizzerias and parks, and learn their histories. If a place really fascinated him, he'd go to the library and dig for information.</p><p>As an adult, the Internet fed his passion.</p><p>In 2011, Mr. Kastanes, inspired by a Facebook page that paid tribute to a shuttered Chicago business, he created one dedicated to the memory of a record store he frequented as a teen.</p><p>In 2012 he created a Facebook page called Chicago Extinct Businesses, later renamed <a class="Link" href="https://www.facebook.com/vanishedchicagoland/" target="_blank" >Vanished Chicagoland</a>. It celebrated things like defunct Chicago businesses and restaurants and invites people to share their memories and favorite forgotten spots.</p><p>He gained a loyal following of nearly 100,000 people on Facebook and hosted a podcast.</p><p>In recent years, he also shared details about his battle with cancer.</p><p>His last Facebook post on April 23 read, in part: "My cancer has spread. I don’t have time much left. As of Vanished Chicagoland the future will be a family decision. Thank you! For my making this fun. I love you all! And god bless!"</p><p>Mr. Kastanes died April 25. He was 62.</p><p>More than 3,000 people commented on his last Facebook post.</p><p>"Vanished Chicagoland wasn't polished, it wasn't some fancy production. It was just Pete sharing what he knew about a TV show or a restaurant or an amusement park, and other people sharing what they knew, and that created a community," said Eric Miller, development coordinator at the Chicago History Museum. "And he was very clear if someone wrote something negative or about politics he'd right away tell everyone 'I won't tolerate it.' And people loved that."</p><p>Mr. Kastanes was born Oct 4, 1963, and grew up in three different South Side neighborhoods: South Shore, Roseland and Ashburn.</p><p>His late father, Chris, was a longtime room service waiter at the downtown Hilton, and his mother, Zoe, was a homemaker and waitress. Both came to the United States from Greece.</p><p>"He's a good person, a good friend, a good son to me," said his mother. "He respected me, respected everybody. He's a good man."</p><p>Mr. Kastanes, a graduate of Bogan High School and DeVry University, lived in Oak Lawn, where he ran Vanished Chicago from his home computer during his free time.</p><p>He worked for American Express Travel, fielding phone calls and assisting customers with their miles and points when booking flights and hotels.</p><p>"It played to his strengths. Pete was friendly and outgoing," said his brother, John Kastanes.</p><p>Following an online groundswell calling for Mr. Kastanes to be recognized for his role in sharing the city's history, the Chicago History Museum created the Citizen History Award and presented it to him during a ceremony in February 2025.</p><p>"It was just a beautiful event, and this is hard for me to say," Miller said, taking a moment. "But a few weeks later he posted on Facebook that it was one of the best days of his life, and it made me feel really good."</p><p>Mr. Kastanes proudly displayed the plaque he received on a wall at his home, his brother said.</p><p>"He was not someone looking for recognition, he just loved it and people loved that about him," Miller said. "He was as Chicago as you can get. He exuded Chicago without pretense."</p><p>His family wasn't sure if Vanished Chicagoland would continue without Mr. Kastanes at the helm.</p><p>A <a class="Link" href="https://orricofuneral.com/pete-kastanes/" target="_blank" >wake will be held Thursday</a> from 3 to 8 p.m. at Palos-Gaidas Funeral Home in Palos Hills. A funeral will be held Friday at 10 a.m. at Saints Constantine & Helen Greek Orthodox Church in Palos Hills.</p>
